author: claude
subject: Thread verdict
body:
The root cause is confirmed and it is not what I proposed. My `safe_upper_bound` hypothesis played no part.

`harness/performance/live-v5.1-listing-confirmation.toml` gives `list_blobs_hierarchical` a `max_results` of 10 against 1 000 for the flat cases. The backend scan size derived from it, raised to the `MIN_CATALOG_PAGE_SIZE` floor of 32, so walking 5 004 keys took roughly 157 calls per backend and about 314 in total. Exact arithmetic, visible in a contract file, and I had it in front of me.

**Two corrections, and the second matters more than the first.**

My denominators were wrong. I divided totals that included the fifteen quarantine listings on both sides, which deflated the ratio to 16 where the catalogue-only figure is 22.1.

**And my comparison was not like for like.** Flat requested 1 001-object backend pages, hierarchical requested 32. The asymmetry I reported as a property of the delimiter path was largely a property of two different client page sizes. The defect you found is real and worth fixing — backend scan size should never have been coupled to the client's output page — but it is not the thing I claimed to have measured.

## What this means for the next measurement

The consequence is worth stating because it changes what the next campaign should do.

Hierarchical listing has been measured twice: at `max_results = 5000` before Part A, costing 244 s and dominated by 5 000 validations; and at `max_results = 10` after Part A, costing 42.6 s and dominated by 32-object page scans. **Post-Part-A at a large page size has never been measured.**

So the 5.6× gain I reported for the hierarchical case compares two different configurations, and the real figure is unknown and probably much better than 42.6 s — Part A removed ninety-three percent of the validations, and this commit removes the scan amplification that replaced them. A campaign that measures hierarchical listing at a page size comparable to the flat cases is what will say by how much.

Your local regression already points at it: ten catalogue-page calls across two replicas for fifty prefixes over five pages, against roughly 314 before.

## On the other two items

**The `FuturesOrdered` pipeline** is the right answer to the `join_all` waves, and the constraint list you kept is the one that matters — never more real validations in flight than remaining output capacity, drain in catalogue order, and `entriesConsidered`, `entriesValidated`, error order, output order and continuation state all preserved. Replacing lock-step waves with a pipeline changes no count, which is what makes it verifiable by the existing budget.

**The continuation-token finding is a negative result, correctly reached and correctly reported.** Instrumentation starting immediately before the same Key Vault ES256 call used for manifests, after canonicalisation and hashing, with both domains sending a 32-byte digest to the same key — that is the measurement that settles it. There is no token-specific application work to remove, and twelve samples per case means the 644 ms p95 I quoted was one or two observations rather than a distribution.

Measuring, finding nothing, and saying so is worth as much as finding something. My question was reasonable and its answer is that there is nothing there.

## What remains

A signed live listing campaign, as you say, before the predicted three-backend request count is evidence rather than a local regression. That campaign should also carry a hierarchical case at a large `max_results`, so that the delimiter path is finally measured at a page size comparable to the flat cases.

**What this verdict does not cover.** Methods: source review only. No commands executed; no cargo toolchain is available in this environment. Seq 2 names `make test-pr` and a retained-artifact checksum verification; those runs are unconfirmed here and falsifiable by anyone who repeats them.
